title: No invented multiplier claims ("10x faster")
summary: Quantified performance claims the model fabricated to fill a stat-led layout, comparison row, or proof bar. Hallmark gate 46 hard-fails invented metrics and antislop R-17/R-36 ban numbers without a real source; a made-up figure is worse than no figure.

source.rule: Gate 46: Invented metric ('10× faster')
R-17 Data & Numbers / R-36 No Fabricated Claims ('300% faster')

tests.label: invented multiplier fails
tests.input: Our platform is 10x faster than the competition.

tests.label: measured claim passes
tests.input: Median API latency dropped from 214ms to 89ms after the 2.4 release.

notes: A real, sourced figure with a named benchmark is not slop; the tell is the round fabricated multiplier. Fix per gate 46: replace with '—' and a labelled grey block, ask the user for the metric, or rebuild the section without the proof slot.

title: No unsourced percentage statistics
summary: Round percentage claims ('+47% conversion', '99.9% uptime') with no source. Hallmark gate 46 lists them as invented metrics; antislop R-17 bans numbers without a real source; No-AI-Slop rule 2 and anti-ai-slop-writing say fake numbers kill trust faster than vagueness.

source.rule: Gate 46: Invented metric ('+47% conversion')
R-17 Data & Numbers
Rule 2: No unsourced statistics
Never invent data, studies, or statistics

tests.label: round conversion stat fails
tests.input: Teams that switch see a +47% conversion lift.

tests.label: sourced number passes
tests.input: Load tests from March 2026 measured peak concurrency at 3,400 requests per second, with the report linked on this page.

notes: Numbers with a named, checkable source (report + date) pass; bare percentages in proof bars fail.

title: No fabricated 'trusted by N+' claims
summary: Trust-bar phrasing ('trusted by 50,000+ teams') is the canonical invented-metric pattern from Hallmark gate 46 and antislop's Fake Statistics list (10K+ Users); it is social proof the model cannot verify.

source.rule: Gate 46: Invented metric ('trusted by 50,000+ teams')
R-17 (Fake Statistics: 10K+ Users) / R-05 ('Trusted By' logo bar)

tests.label: trust count fails
tests.input: Trusted by 50,000+ teams worldwide.

tests.label: verifiable customer reference passes
tests.input: Featured in the customer story with Northwind Logistics (2026 case study, PDF).

notes: Applies to proof bars, hero sublines, and footer trust strips. A link to a real, verifiable customer reference is not a violation.

title: No unsourced user/scale counts
summary: Bare round counts ('10K+ users', '500M requests', '120+ countries') without a source appear in antislop's Fake Statistics list and violate R-17 and No-AI-Slop rule 2.

source.rule: R-17 (Fake Statistics: 10K+ Users, 500M Requests, 120+ Countries)
Rule 2: No unsourced statistics

tests.label: bare count fails
tests.input: Serving 500M requests and 120+ countries.

tests.label: counted source passes
tests.input: Per our 2025 transparency report: 1.2M monthly requests.

title: No fabricated testimonials or social proof
summary: Fictional reviews, invented names and job titles, AI avatars, and generic 'Trusted By' logo bars are hard-banned by antislop R-18 and R-38 (real content or honest placeholder) and the Evidence Over Claims standard (C-5).

source.rule: R-18 Testimonials / R-38 Real Content or Honest Placeholder / C-5 Evidence Over Claims

tests.label: invented review fails
tests.input: "This product changed my life." — Sarah K., Marketing Director

tests.label: real testimonial passes
tests.input: "Migration took four hours, not four weeks." — verified quote from the Northwind Logistics case study, linked on this page.

notes: If there are no real testimonials, do not create a testimonials section at all (R-18). A testimonial is real only when it traces to a verifiable source.

title: No fabricated compliance/security claims
summary: Certification and security claims ('SOC 2 compliant', 'ISO 27001', 'enterprise-grade security') are forbidden without real evidence (antislop R-36; also R-17 and C-5).

source.rule: R-36 No Fabricated Claims ('SOC 2 compliant', 'ISO 27001', '300% faster')
Gate 46 (security claims must be user-supplied)

tests.label: unsupported cert fails
tests.input: SOC 2 compliant with enterprise-grade security.

tests.label: evidence-linked cert passes
tests.input: SOC 2 Type II report (2025) available for download in the trust center.

notes: A claim backed by a link to the actual report is not fabrication; the bare badge is.

title: No fabricated attributions or quotes
summary: Never claim a person, organization, or company said something unless it is real and verifiable; quoting someone without a real source is fabrication and a defamation risk (No-AI-Slop rule 19). Anti-ai-slop-writing likewise bans fabricating quotes, and rule 23 requires quotes to match the source exactly.

source.rule: Rule 19: No fabricated attributions / Rule 23: Quote sources accurately
Never fabricate quotes; paraphrase with attribution or skip it

tests.label: invented attribution fails
tests.input: Industry analyst Gartner argues that legacy systems are the main cost driver.

tests.label: sourced attribution passes
tests.input: In its March 2026 report, Gartner writes: "Legacy systems account for the largest share of IT cost."

notes: Every attributed quote or position must trace to a real document, transcript, public statement, or report. Altered quotes need square brackets; otherwise paraphrase without quotation marks.

title: Placeholders must be explicitly labeled
summary: Real content or an honest placeholder: filler text (Lorem ipsum, TBD) shipped as final violates antislop R-38, and placeholder statistics must be marked [REAL DATA] per R-23.

source.rule: R-38 Real Content or Honest Placeholder / R-23 (statistics marked [REAL DATA])

tests.label: unlabeled filler fails
tests.input: Hero stat: Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet (10K+ users).

tests.label: labeled placeholder passes
tests.input: Statistic: [REAL DATA] — pending measurement.

notes: An explicitly labeled placeholder ([REAL DATA], 'Coming soon') is honest and allowed; the same content disguised as final is fabrication (R-38).

title: No placeholder names or startup clichés
summary: Hallmark gate 19 flags placeholder names ('Jane Doe / John Smith') and startup clichés (Acme, Nexus, Seamless, Unleash); antislop R-18 and R-23 ban invented names and identities in testimonials and assets.

source.rule: Gate 19: placeholder name 'Jane Doe / John Smith' or startup cliché
R-18 Testimonials / R-23 Clarification & Visual Assets

tests.label: placeholder name fails
tests.input: "Acme's platform saved us weeks" — Jane Doe, VP Engineering

tests.label: real identity passes
tests.input: In the customer story: Mariam Diallo, platform lead at Northwind Logistics.

notes: Warning tier: these names are legitimate in docs/examples with an explicit 'example' marker; they are slop in final product copy. Real, named customers replace the placeholders.

title: No fabricated case studies or invented anecdotes
summary: Narrative scenarios presented as real events — invented outcomes, actions, or stories — are forbidden by No-AI-Slop rule 17; anti-ai-slop-writing says fabricated specificity is worse than honest vagueness (use 'imagine'/'suppose' for hypotheticals).

source.rule: Rule 17: No fabricated case studies or scenarios
Never invent anecdotes or present hypotheticals as real

tests.label: invented scenario fails
tests.input: When Acme's data team adopted the platform, their query time fell 80% in a week.

tests.label: explicit hypothetical passes
tests.input: Suppose a data team moves 4TB of parquet nightly; the platform pipelines it in about nine minutes.

title: No fabricated history, dates, or milestones
summary: Inventing dates for events, launches, founding, or milestones is forbidden by No-AI-Slop rule 18; every date and event must be real.

source.rule: Rule 18: No fabricated history or milestones

tests.label: invented milestone fails
tests.input: Founded in 2019, the company has shipped 40 releases every quarter since.

tests.label: documented date passes
tests.input: First public release: 2023-11-14 (CHANGELOG.md).

title: No vague citations ('research shows')
summary: Unverifiable citation hedges — 'research shows', 'studies indicate', 'according to experts' — stand in for real sources. Anti-ai-slop-writing requires real verifiable names ('a Databricks report from March 2026' beats 'research shows'), and No-AI-Slop rule 2 bans unsourced statistics.

source.rule: Use real verifiable names, companies, dates ('research shows' banned)
Rule 2: No unsourced statistics

tests.label: vague citation fails
tests.input: Research shows that most teams struggle with data quality.

tests.label: named source passes
tests.input: A Databricks report from March 2026 found that 61% of teams cite data quality as their top blocker.

notes: Warning tier: the hedge is the tell. Replace it with a named, dated, checkable source or cut the claim.

title: No decorative stats in stat-led layouts
summary: A stat-led proof bar is slop the moment its stats become decorative (Hallmark gate 46); antislop R-05 bans 'Hero + fake stats' layouts where the numbers exist only to fill the template.

source.rule: Gate 46: stat-led macrostructures are slop the moment stats become decorative
R-05 (Hero + fake stats forbidden)

tests.label: decorative stat grid fails
tests.input: Hero proof bar: 99.9% uptime · 10x faster · +47% conversion — no sources anywhere on the page.

tests.label: content-driven section passes
tests.input: Section with one measured number and a link to the report that produced it.

notes: Judge the layout, not just individual claims: three unsourced numbers in a row are the pattern.

title: A stat is never the hero's sole headline
summary: Hallmark gate 46: a lead figure carries the hero only alongside a worded headline; a giant number with no words as the dominant hero text is a slop tell even before the number's provenance is questioned.

source.rule: Gate 46: a stat is also never the hero's sole headline

tests.label: bare stat hero fails
tests.input: Hero = giant "99.9%" with a one-line sub and no worded headline.

tests.label: worded hero passes
tests.input: Hero headline: "Reliable builds, measured" with a supporting stat below.

title: No assumed logos, avatars, or photos
summary: Creating app logos, avatars, profile photos, or people imagery without explicit instructions is banned by antislop R-23: ask first, or use clear placeholders that are not disguised as final.

source.rule: R-23 Clarification & Visual Assets (Assumed Logo & Profile Photos)

tests.label: invented avatar fails
tests.input: Generated a photorealistic team page with five invented faces and names.

tests.label: placeholder passes
tests.input: Team avatars are initial-based placeholders labeled as placeholders until the user supplies photos.

title: No chat-tool citation or footnote artifacts
summary: Internal citation tokens that leak through when text is copy-pasted from chat UIs — citeturn0search1, turn0image0, oai_citation, [attached_file:1], [web:1], and the ↩ footnote character — are fingerprints, not patterns: their presence is essentially proof the text came from a specific chat tool and was pasted without cleanup (avoid-ai-writing 'Chatbot citation markup leaks'; ai-writing-detection Markup Red Flags).

source.rule: Chatbot citation markup leaks
Markup Red Flags (definitive) — turn0search/turn0image, oai_citation, footnote markers
ChatGPT-specific artifacts: citeturn0searchN, turn0imageN, oai_citation
Footnote markers (↩ / ↩2) at the end of citations

tests.label: leaked citation token fails
tests.input: The school is also a center for the US College Board examinations citeturn0search1.

tests.label: clean citation passes
tests.input: The school also hosts the US College Board examinations; details are on the official website.

notes: The core tokens oaicite / contentReference / grok_card / attributableIndex are enforced by the prose-domain 'Hallucinated markup artifacts' rule; this rule catches the numeric variants (citeturn0search1, turn0image0, turn0news0) and the Grok/Perplexity/footnote artifacts that rule misses. The ↩ marker is U+21A9.

title: No AI-tool tracking parameters in URLs
summary: utm_source=chatgpt.com (pre-August 2025), utm_source=openai (current), and utm_source=copilot.com are tracking parameters chat tools auto-append to cited URLs; their presence definitively proves tool involvement (ai-writing-detection utm_source Tracking; avoid-ai-writing 'AI-tool URL parameters').

source.rule: utm_source Tracking (utm_source=chatgpt.com / utm_source=openai)
AI-tool URL parameters

tests.label: chatgpt tracking param fails
tests.input: See the full report at https://www.theguardian.com/tech/article?utm_source=chatgpt.com.

tests.label: clean URL passes
tests.input: See the full report at https://www.theguardian.com/tech/article.

notes: The parameter proves the tool was used to find the citation, not necessarily that it wrote the prose. Fix: strip the tracking parameter and keep the URL if the link matters.

title: No zero-width characters in prose
summary: Zero-width characters (ZWSP U+200B, ZWNJ U+200C, ZWJ U+200D, BOM U+FEFF, word joiner U+2060) are inserted by AI-humanizer bypass tools to defeat exact-match detection; humans do not type them (avoid-ai-writing 'normalization-flag': 'Text contains invisible/lookalike chars typical of AI-humanizer bypass tools').

source.rule: normalization-flag — Zero-width / homoglyph humanizer-bypass detection
v2: zero-width chars trigger normalization-flag

tests.label: zero-width spacer fails
tests.input: Our team shipped a fix on Monday​ afternoon and the deploy is green.

tests.label: clean text passes
tests.input: Our team shipped a fix on Monday afternoon and the deploy is green.

notes: A single occurrence can be copy-paste residue from Word/Notion; two or more are near-dispositive (the detector's strong-corroborator threshold is ≥2). Fix: re-type from your own keyboard.

title: No homoglyph lookalikes in Latin text
summary: Cyrillic/Greek letters visually identical to Latin (Cyrillic е о р с у х а) are swapped into words to defeat exact-match AI detectors; the detector normalizes them and flags the swap (avoid-ai-writing homoglyph normalization: 'dеlve' with Cyrillic 'е' would not equal 'delve' before normalization).

source.rule: Cyrillic homoglyph swap restores Tier 1 hit; ≥2 homoglyphs trigger normalization-flag
normalization-flag — Zero-width / homoglyph humanizer-bypass detection

tests.label: cyrillic e swaps fail
tests.input: Dеlvе into the details of the report before you ship.

tests.label: latin text passes
tests.input: Delve into the details of the report before you ship.

notes: High false-positive risk in Russian, Ukrainian, and other Cyrillic-script text — apply only to Latin-dominant prose and require ≥2 swaps before flagging (single occurrences are legitimate in mixed-script content).

title: No unfilled bracketed slot-fillers
summary: Bracketed slot-fillers meant to be replaced before publishing — [Your Name], [INSERT SOURCE URL], [Describe the specific section], date stubs like 2025-XX-XX, and HTML comments with placeholder verbs — are near-definitive evidence that AI-generated boilerplate was pasted without editing (avoid-ai-writing 'Unfilled placeholders'; ai-writing-detection Placeholder Text Artifacts).

source.rule: Unfilled placeholders
ai-placeholder detector (slot-fill brackets, date stubs, HTML comment placeholders)
Placeholder Text Artifacts: [Describe the specific section...], access-date=2025-XX-XX

tests.label: slot-filler and date stub fail
tests.input: Dear [Recipient], I am writing regarding [Topic of Discussion]. Last updated 2025-XX-XX.

tests.label: real bracketed content passes
tests.input: The release notes for [v1.2.3] cover the [auth.refresh] path and reference [@example/user].

notes: Extends ZS-INTEGRITY-008 (filler words: lorem ipsum / TBD) to bracket slot-fillers and date stubs. The regex is gated on placeholder verbs (Your/Insert/Add/...) so real bracketed content like [v1.2.3] or [@user] never matches. Treat any visible placeholder as a publishing bug: fill it with real content or delete the sentence.

title: No vague third-party validation
summary: AI manufactures credibility by pointing at an unnamed external authority with a generic superlative — 'independent testing confirms', 'third-party benchmarks show we lead', 'analysts agree', 'studies consistently show' — the authority is faceless and the claim unfalsifiable (avoid-ai-writing 'Vague third-party validation': name the source, the test, and the result or cut the claim).

source.rule: Vague third-party validation

tests.label: unnamed authority fails
tests.input: Independent testing confirms our platform leads the market, and analysts agree.

tests.label: named checkable source passes
tests.input: On Stanford's HELM leaderboard (April 2026 run), we ranked first on reasoning latency.

notes: Extends ZS-INTEGRITY-012 (research shows / experts say) to the manufactured-authority family. Specifically attributed, checkable validation stays unflagged — a named benchmark, a linked report, a dated audit. The tell is the vagueness, not the act of citing outside proof.

title: No injected voice moves (never-inject list)
summary: Putting voice back on purpose has a predictable failure mode: the model installs a stock personality the author never had. Manufactured stakes ('in a world where', 'now more than ever'), forced contrarianism, performed candor ('real talk', 'let's be honest'), and fake first person ('in my experience', 'I've seen this a hundred times') are out of bounds — the source had no I, so the rewrite has no I (avoid-ai-writing 'Never inject these').

terms: the stakes have never been higher
i've seen this a hundred times

source.rule: Never inject these — fake first person, manufactured stakes, forced contrarianism, performed candor, invented specifics

tests.label: manufactured stakes fails
tests.input: In a world where data teams struggle daily, the stakes have never been higher for analytics tools.

tests.label: grounded claim passes
tests.input: Data teams spend roughly a quarter of their week moving data between systems.

notes: These phrases are banned as ADDITIONS during a rewrite; the governing test is provenance — did the information come from the source? In detection, a hit is a warning, not proof: the phrase alone is legitimate in human prose with real author presence. 'Here's the thing' and 'I'll be honest' are enforced by the prose throat-clearing rule. 'Invented specifics' (a number, name, date, or tool the source never contained) is semantic and deferred to M3.

title: No model-generated Unsplash image URLs
summary: Direct-embed Unsplash URLs (images.unsplash.com/photo-<id>) generated by models frequently 404 — the model interpolates a plausible photo ID that does not resolve. Taste-design and stitch-design-taste ban broken Unsplash links and require picsum.photos or SVG avatars instead.

source.rule: No broken Unsplash links — use picsum.photos or SVG avatars
No broken Unsplash links — use picsum.photos or SVG avatars

tests.label: photo-id embed fails
picsum placeholder passes

notes: Targets the direct-embed photo-<id> pattern that models interpolate; a real, verified Unsplash page link (unsplash.com/photos/…) is not a violation.

title: TTR floor 0.40 on 200+ word prose
summary: Type-token ratio (distinct word types ÷ total tokens) on general English prose over ~200 words usually lands around 0.50–0.65; AI text trends flatter, sometimes drifting under 0.40 when the model locks onto a small vocabulary loop (avoid-ai-writing TTR: 'a TTR below 0.40 is worth a second look').

source.rule: TTR / low vocabulary diversity (low-ttr)

tests.label: varied prose passes
tests.input: The first deployment I ever shipped took eleven hours and a fire extinguisher. The monitoring dashboard showed the queue backing up in real time, and nobody knew why until someone spotted the connection-pool leak in the log. We rolled back, fixed the default, and redeployed in four minutes. That is the difference the current pipeline makes: a feedback loop measured in minutes instead of days. The design principles came from the incident log, not from a template. Every environment gets its own database, its own credentials, and its own alert thresholds, because shared infrastructure turned out to be shared blame. The weekly on-call rotation keeps ownership honest, and the postmortem habit means the same failure rarely appears twice. Metrics are named after the business outcome they protect, so a spike in checkout latency reads as lost revenue, not as a graph nobody understands. The runbook is short on purpose: if a step needs explaining, the explanation belongs in the code. Nobody memorizes the recovery procedure; they read it aloud during the incident, which is how the inaccuracies get found. Small teams ship this way without ceremony, and the tools we built are boring by design — no magic, just fast feedback and honest numbers.

notes: Not proof by itself — narrow topics, technical reference material, and second-language writing legitimately compress vocabulary. The fix is rarely to thesaurus the text; it is to name specific things and replace a re-used abstract noun with the concrete instance behind it.

title: Detection verdicts need corroborating signals
summary: Never flag on a single indicator: 'This says delve so it's AI' is the canonical false positive. Minimum 2–3 corroborating signals from different categories (vocabulary AND structure AND/OR statistical features) before any flag, and 4+ across categories plus no strong mitigating factors for a 'likely AI' assessment (ai-writing-detection false-positive prevention).

source.rule: Signal requirements — no single indicator ever sufficient; 2–3 corroborating signals minimum
Key principles — multiple signals required; single indicators prove nothing

notes: Single-indicator verdicts are the top false-positive source. Weight vocabulary signals lower for ESL contexts, apply domain-adjusted thresholds, and always check mitigating factors (personal anecdotes, idiomatic language, minor errors) before reporting.

title: No literal parameter placeholders in citations
summary: Citation templates with the parameter name repeated as its own value — url=URL, website=Website — are fill-in-the-blank stubs the model generated and the author never completed; ai-writing-detection rates the literal 'URL' placeholder 'Very High' confidence.

source.rule: URL placeholder patterns — literal 'URL' placeholder (|url=URL)

tests.label: url=URL stub fails

tests.label: real citation passes

notes: Pairs with ZS-INTEGRITY-020 for the date-stub half of the same template pattern. Full citation verification — broken external links, DOI/ISBN checksum failures, declared-but-unused references — is semantic/network-dependent and deferred to M3.
